pages.text: Stars and Galaxies

image.note: Cover: a night sky ablaze with stars and a spiral galaxy

pages.text: Contents. Looking Up / What Is a Star? / The Life of a Star / Galaxies / How Far Away? / Are We Alone?

Go outside on a clear, dark night, far from the city lights, and look up. The sky is scattered with thousands of stars, more than you could ever count. People have gazed at them for as long as there have been people, and asked the same questions you are asking now. What are they? How far? And are we alone?

image.note: A child gazing up at a sky full of stars

pages.text: For most of history, nobody knew. The stars were mysteries, used to tell stories and find directions. But little by little, clever people worked out the truth, and it turned out to be more astonishing than any story. The tiny lights in the sky are giant, blazing suns, so far away that their light takes years to reach your eyes.

image.note: Ancient stargazers beside a modern telescope

pages.text: A star is an enormous ball of burning gas, so vast and so hot that it shines with its own light across the whole of space. The tiny twinkling points you see are not small at all. They only look small because they are unimaginably far away.

image.note: A star shown as a vast ball of glowing gas

pages.text: How can we be so sure? Because you know one star very well already. The Sun, which lights your days and warms your world, is a star, our own star, close enough to fill the sky. Every other star is a sun like ours, some smaller, some far larger, each one blazing away in the dark.

image.note: The Sun beside a distant star, shown as the same kind of thing

pages.text: Deep in the heart of a star, the heat and pressure are so tremendous that the star makes its own light and warmth, in a way no fire on earth can match. It is this that keeps a star shining, steadily, for millions upon millions of years, pouring light out into space in every direction.

image.note: The blazing core of a star

pages.text: Stars are born, live, and die, though their lives are so long that to us they seem to last for ever. A star begins in a vast cloud of gas and dust, drifting in space. Slowly, over ages, gravity pulls the cloud together, tighter and tighter, until at its heart a new star flickers into light.

image.note: A star being born in a cloud of gas and dust

pages.text: Once lit, a star shines for a very, very long time, often billions of years, steady and bright. Our own Sun is about halfway through its long life. It was shining long before there was any life on earth, and it will go on shining long after, giving light and warmth all the while.

image.note: A steady, shining star over a long span of time

pages.text: But no star shines for ever. When at last a star runs low on fuel, it changes. Some swell up huge and red, then quietly fade. Others, the very biggest, end in a tremendous explosion called a supernova, blazing for a time brighter than a whole galaxy, before scattering their dust back into space, where one day new stars will be born.

image.note: A giant star ending in a bright supernova

pages.text: Stars are not scattered evenly through space. They gather together, in their billions, into great islands of stars called galaxies, held together by gravity, turning slowly through the dark. Our own Sun, and every star you can see with your eyes, belongs to one such island.

image.note: A great spiral galaxy of countless stars

pages.text: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way, and on a very dark night you can see it: a faint, milky band of light stretching across the sky, which is the glow of its countless stars, too far and too many to tell apart. Every single star you have ever seen is one of its family.

image.note: The Milky Way as a band of light across the sky

pages.text: And here is the truly staggering part. The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars. And it is only one galaxy. Out in space there are billions of other galaxies, each with its own billions of stars. The numbers are so vast that no one can truly picture them. The universe is larger than the mind can hold.

image.note: Countless galaxies scattered across the universe

pages.text: The stars are so far away that ordinary numbers are useless. So we measure their distance in a special way, by how long their light takes to reach us. Light is the fastest thing there is, crossing from the Sun to the earth in about eight minutes. A distance that light takes a whole year to cross is called a light-year.

image.note: A beam of light travelling from a star to the earth

pages.text: The nearest star beyond the Sun is over four light-years away. Its light, racing towards you all this time, left it more than four years ago. And that is the closest one. The light of other stars has been travelling for hundreds, or thousands, of years before it reaches your eyes tonight.

image.note: Starlight travelling for years across space

pages.text: This means something wonderful and strange. When you look up at the stars, you are looking into the past. The light you see left those stars long ago, and has been crossing the dark ever since. Some of the stars you see may even have died already, and yet their old light still shines on, on its long way to you.

image.note: A child looking up, the starlight arriving from the past

pages.text: With so many billions of stars, and so many of them circled by worlds of their own, people have long wondered: is there life out there? On some far planet, around some distant star, could there be creatures looking up at their own night sky, wondering the very same thing about us?

image.note: A distant planet with an unknown sky

pages.text: Nobody knows. So far, we have found life only here, on our own small world. But we have searched only the tiniest corner of a universe almost beyond counting. The question is one of the greatest we have, and it is still, gloriously, unanswered. Perhaps, one day, someone of your time will help to answer it.

image.note: Earth as one small world in a vast starry universe

pages.text: So the next time you stand under a clear night sky, remember what you are really seeing: not tiny lights, but distant suns, gathered into vast islands, their ancient light arriving after a journey of years. You are looking out across almost unimaginable distance, and back across almost unimaginable time.

image.note: A child small beneath an enormous, glittering sky

pages.text: Words to know. Star: a giant ball of burning gas that shines with its own light. Supernova: the great explosion that ends the largest stars. Galaxy: an island of billions of stars. The Milky Way: our own galaxy. Light-year: the distance light travels in one year.

image.note: Labelled diagram: star, galaxy, light-year

pages.text: The nearest star of all is one you see every day, so close it lights your whole world: the Sun. It is the star we know best, and the one our lives depend upon. Turn the page of your reading, and go and meet it.

image.note: The Sun, our nearest star, rising
